🍎 Lesson plan · 🤿 Deep dive · Lesson 11

Lesson plan: Can You Trust AI?

How AI gets things wrong, how it is tested, how to protect your data, and the rules that are appearing for AI.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • name three ways AI goes wrong: bias, hallucination and overconfidence;
  • explain why one accuracy number is not enough, and how testing by group and red teaming help;
  • protect their own data, and describe how laws such as the EU AI Act sort AI uses by risk.

Warm-up

A face-unlock system is right 95% of the time. Would you trust it? What else would you want to know?

Most students will say yes. Leave the question open: the exit ticket comes back to it at the end.

Reading

Students read the lesson “Can You Trust AI?”. Students look for the three ways AI goes wrong, what the Gender Shades study found, and what “social scoring” is.

Activity: Mini-lab “Fair or not?”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 11: four short cases.
  2. In pairs, they discuss each case and agree on an answer before they click.
  3. In the face-unlock case, they split the results by skin tone and compare the numbers.
  4. For each case, they write on the worksheet what would help.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers invent a fifth case from school life (for example, an AI that marks homework), and write what could go wrong and how to test it.

Discussion questions

  • Who should decide whether an AI is fair enough to use: the company, the government or the people it affects?
  • Why is it dangerous to punish a student because an AI detector said their essay was written by AI?
  • What would you never type into a chatbot? Has this lesson changed your answer?
  • The EU AI Act bans “social scoring”. Why do you think lawmakers banned it?

Exit ticket

Give one way to test an AI fairly, other than looking at one accuracy number.

Quick check. A face-unlock system is right 95% of the time in tests. Why might that not be good enough?
Right answer: It may fail much more often for some groups of people

Easier and harder

Easier. Work through the first case together on the projector, then let pairs do the other three.

Harder. Students design a fair test for an AI that understands spoken commands: which groups of speakers they would include, which unusual situations they would try, and which results they would report.
